extracted.intended_audience: student journalists / novice reporters (high school & college journalism students)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on grammatical ways to begin news leads and a step-by-step method for reporting speeches, aimed at teaching students how to construct effective leads and organize speech reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Noun clause beginning with that/how/why/what/whether
rubrics_metrics.description: To play up a summary of a result, opinion, or statement, used as subject of the main verb.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show leads that begin with 'That the low point ... has been reached is indicated by reports...' and diplomatic/news examples: 'That the United States has lined up with Great Britain...' Use this form to foreground a summary statement or reported opinion as the subject. (Examples provided from Paris and Nashville datelines.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinitive beginning (To ...)
rubrics_metrics.description: To play up action as the subject of the main verb or to play up purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use an infinitive at the start to emphasize the action/purpose: e.g., 'To cleanse the world of leprosy ... is the aim of Governor General Leonard Wood.' Also used to place purpose in the lead (journalism typically does not use 'in order that'). Examples and exercises demonstrate using infinitives to highlight purpose or result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clause of cause beginning with because/since/as
rubrics_metrics.description: To play up cause or motive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sparingly (the text cautions 'This must not be used too often'). Examples: 'Because the Sioux Tribe ... a new form of Indian warfare is likely to break out...' or human-interest rescues where cause explains outcome. Use when cause/motive is the point to highlight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adverbial clause of concession (although/though/while)
rubrics_metrics.description: To play up an obstacle overcome (seldom used).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use to emphasize an obstacle that was overcome; examples include market or political stories that qualify a positive development with an obstacle. The text marks this as seldom used and shows examples from markets and legislative processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditional clause beginning with if/unless/not or equivalent
rubrics_metrics.description: To play up speculation or significant conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use conditional leads to foreground speculation or conditions affecting an outcome: e.g., 'If the Harvard oarsmen cut as much ice ... the Crimson-oared shell should be under the flotilla whistles first next June.' Also 'Unless further investigation ... the commission may consider...' Works for hypothetical or contingent situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nominative absolute
rubrics_metrics.description: To play up attendant human-interest description or to give antecedent circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to add descriptive background or human-interest detail; the book notes high school students should recognize but not use. Example: funeral over, attention turned to Parliament...

rubrics_metrics.name: Adverbial clause of time beginning with when/while/before/after
rubrics_metrics.description: To play up action attending the main event when the time of the action is more important than the main event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marked as a form high school students should 'recognize but never use.' Examples include accident reports or events where timing/detail of attendant action is the story's focus. Use when the timing/attendant action is the most newsworthy element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify speaker by role relevant to subject
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting a speech, identify the speaker by the role that gives weight to the statements (the capacity in which the speaker speaks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note: if the chairman of the scholarship committee is head of the art department and is speaking on scholarships, identify her as chairman of the scholarship committee (her words have weight as chairman). Avoid cumbersome characterizations but choose the identification that conveys authority on the topic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Before the speech — preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: Get the full name of the speaker, his subject, and facts that identify him as an authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect identification and contextual facts in advance so the report can open with a clear summary lead that establishes who spoke, why they matter, and on what occasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: During the speech — note-taking
rubrics_metrics.description: The speech will contain much more material than you can use; take notes on the highlights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus notes on high points and memorable lines that will serve as direct or indirect quotations. Don't attempt to record everything verbatim; capture the gist and the most newsworthy or vivid passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: After the speech — review and summarize
rubrics_metrics.description: Review your facts. Decide which to include in a summary that will give the gist of the talk. When you begin to write, put this summary at the beginning of your report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The lead should give the gist of the talk; verbatim reports may transcribe steno notes but are not the journalistic method. Emphasize significance and compress the speech into its newsworthy core.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speech report organization formula
rubrics_metrics.description: A simple formula for organizing a speech report: 1) summary lead (title/nature/speaker identification/occasion), 2) direct quotation for vividness, 3) indirect quotation for economy and variety, 4) direct quotation to conclude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use direct quotes sparingly for impact and indirect quotes to compress and explain. Any significant audience reaction may be noted. The writer's taste determines proportion of direct vs. indirect quotations according to speech length.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid verbatim transcription as the primary method
rubrics_metrics.description: A verbatim report may be a good transcription of stenographic notes, but it is not the journalistic method of reporting a speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The journalist should select and summarize significant material rather than present the entire speech verbatim; put significance in the lead and compress material for readers who did not attend.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep the speaker before the reader
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep the speaker in the mind of your readers by referring to him throughout the report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain clarity about who is speaking; refer back to the speaker so readers can follow attribution and authority. This helps readers who both did and did not attend.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution — don't mix direct and indirect discourse in one paragraph
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid mixing direct and indirect quotation styles within the same paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate direct quotes (verbatim speech) and indirect paraphrase into different paragraphs for clarity and economy. This improves flow and prevents confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution — vary the verb 'said'
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't use 'said' too often; have a list of synonyms ready.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use alternative attribution verbs tactfully (e.g., 'added', 'noted', 'urged') to avoid repetition, but don’t overdo elaborate or inappropriate verbs; choose synonyms that fit the tone and accuracy of the attribution.
